notes:
1. Meaning of Communalism

  • Communalism in modern Indian politics refers to the political mobilisation of religious communities as separate political interests.
  • It gradually encouraged the belief that different religious communities required separate political representation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Communalism → Religion Used as a Basis of Political Mobilisation

2. Communalism and Religion

  • Religion by itself is not the same as communalism.
  • Communalism arises when religious identity is converted into an exclusive political identity or competing political interest.

3. Colonial Context

  • Communal politics developed under complex conditions involving:
    • Colonial policies.
    • Representative institutions.
    • Competition for jobs and education.
    • Elite political rivalry.
    • Religious reform movements.
    • Electoral arrangements.

4. British Policy

  • British policies frequently encouraged separate political representation based on community.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Colonial Constitutional Reforms → Institutionalised Communal Representation

5. Divide and Rule

  • "Divide and Rule" is commonly used to describe British attempts to exploit political and social divisions within India.

6. Separate Political Interests

  • As representative institutions expanded, political leaders increasingly debated whether representation should be based on:
    • Territory.
    • Population.
    • Community.

7. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan

  • Sir Syed Ahmad Khan was an important nineteenth-century Muslim reformer and educationist.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sir Syed Ahmad Khan → Aligarh Movement

8. Aligarh Movement

  • The Aligarh Movement sought modern education and social advancement among Indian Muslims.

9. Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College

  • Sir Syed founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in 1875.
📌 Must-Memorise

MAO College → Aligarh → 1875

10. Aligarh Muslim University

  • The MAO College later developed into Aligarh Muslim University.

11. Sir Syed and Congress

  • Sir Syed was critical of the early Indian National Congress.
  • He feared that representative government based purely on numerical majority could disadvantage Muslims.

12. Early Political Separation

  • Such concerns contributed to the later development of separate political organisations and demands.

13. Hindi–Urdu Controversy

  • Language disputes, particularly the Hindi–Urdu controversy in northern India, contributed to sharper community-based political identities.

14. Cow-Protection Disputes

  • Religious mobilisation around cow protection also produced Hindu-Muslim tensions in parts of northern India in the late nineteenth century.

15. Religious Reform and Identity

  • Organisations promoting religious reform sometimes strengthened community consciousness even when their original goals were primarily social or religious.

16. Partition of Bengal

  • Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905.
📌 Must-Memorise

Partition of Bengal → 1905 → Lord Curzon

17. Bengal Partition and Politics

  • The Partition of Bengal produced:
    • Swadeshi.
    • Boycott.
    • Mass nationalist agitation.
  • It also affected communal political alignments in eastern Bengal.

18. Eastern Bengal and Assam

  • A new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam was created in 1905.

19. Muslim Elite Support

  • Some Muslim elites in eastern Bengal initially supported the new province because they expected greater administrative and political opportunities.

20. Anti-Partition Movement

  • The Congress-led anti-partition movement became a major nationalist mobilisation.

21. Simla Deputation

  • A delegation of prominent Muslim leaders met Viceroy Lord Minto at Simla in 1906.
📌 Must-Memorise

Simla Deputation → 1906

22. Aga Khan

  • The Simla Deputation was led by Aga Khan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Simla Deputation → Aga Khan

23. Main Demand

  • The deputation demanded separate political representation for Muslims.

24. Weightage

  • Muslim representatives also sought representation that would reflect political importance rather than merely numerical population in some contexts.

25. Significance of Simla Deputation

  • The deputation strengthened the demand for a distinct Muslim political constituency.

26. All-India Muslim League

  • The All-India Muslim League was founded at Dacca in December 1906.
📌 Must-Memorise

Muslim League → Dacca → 1906

27. Dacca

  • Present-day Dhaka in Bangladesh was then part of Eastern Bengal.

28. Nawab Salimullah

  • Nawab Salimullah of Dacca played an important role in the formation of the Muslim League.

29. Viqar-ul-Mulk

  • Viqar-ul-Mulk was another prominent figure associated with its early organisation.

30. Aga Khan

  • Aga Khan became one of the League's leading early personalities.

31. Early Objectives of Muslim League

The League initially sought to:

  • Promote loyalty to the British government.
  • Protect Muslim political rights.
  • Represent Muslim political interests.

32. League's Early Character

  • The early Muslim League was largely an elite political organisation.
  • It did not initially demand Pakistan.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Muslim League Founded 1906 ≠ Pakistan Demand Began in 1906

33. Morley–Minto Reforms

  • The Indian Councils Act of 1909 is commonly known as the Morley–Minto Reforms.
📌 Must-Memorise

Morley–Minto Reforms → 1909

34. John Morley

  • John Morley was the Secretary of State for India.

35. Lord Minto

  • Lord Minto was the Viceroy.

36. Separate Electorates

  • The 1909 reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
📌 Must-Memorise

Separate Electorates for Muslims → 1909

37. Meaning of Separate Electorate

  • Under a separate electorate, members of a particular community voted for representatives belonging to that community.

38. Political Effect

  • Separate electorates formally incorporated religious identity into the electoral system.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

1909 → Communal Representation Institutionalised

39. Annulment of Bengal Partition

  • The Partition of Bengal was annulled in 1911.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bengal Partition → 1905, Annulled → 1911

40. Capital Shift

  • In 1911, the capital of British India was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi.

41. Congress–League Cooperation

  • Despite separate political organisations, Congress and the Muslim League periodically cooperated.

42. Muhammad Ali Jinnah

  • Muhammad Ali Jinnah initially participated in both broader nationalist politics and constitutional cooperation between Congress and the League.

43. Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity

  • Jinnah was once popularly described as an "Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity."
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Early Jinnah → Constitutional Cooperation, Later Jinnah → Pakistan Demand

44. Lucknow Session

  • Congress and the Muslim League reached an important agreement at Lucknow in 1916.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lucknow Pact → 1916

45. Lucknow Pact

  • The agreement is known as the Lucknow Pact.

46. Congress Acceptance

  • Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims as part of the agreement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lucknow Pact → Congress Accepted Separate Electorates

47. League Cooperation

  • The Muslim League joined Congress in demanding constitutional reforms.

48. Political Importance

  • The Lucknow Pact represented a high point of Congress-League cooperation.

49. Weightage Principle

  • The agreement also accepted special representation or weightage for Muslims in certain provinces.

50. Tilak and Lucknow

  • Bal Gangadhar Tilak supported the Congress-League rapprochement.

51. Jinnah and Lucknow

  • Jinnah played an important role in the constitutional negotiations of this period.

52. Khilafat Movement

  • The Khilafat Movement emerged after World War I over the future of the Ottoman Caliphate.

53. Gandhi and Khilafat

  • Gandhi supported the Khilafat cause and linked it with Non-Cooperation.

54. Hindu-Muslim Unity

  • The combined Khilafat–Non-Cooperation phase temporarily strengthened Hindu-Muslim political cooperation.

55. Ali Brothers

  • Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali were major Khilafat leaders.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ali Brothers → Khilafat Movement

56. End of Khilafat Issue

  • The abolition of the Ottoman Caliphate in 1924 removed the central international issue behind the Khilafat Movement.

57. Communal Tensions in the 1920s

  • The 1920s witnessed increased communal tension and riots in several parts of India.

58. Shuddhi

  • Shuddhi campaigns sought reconversion into Hindu society.

59. Sangathan

  • Sangathan emphasised Hindu communal organisation and consolidation.

60. Tabligh and Tanzim

  • Muslim religious mobilisation also developed through movements such as Tabligh and Tanzim.

61. Political Polarisation

  • Competing religious mobilisation contributed to deteriorating Hindu-Muslim political relations.

62. Hindu Mahasabha

  • The All-India Hindu Mahasabha emerged as an important organisation representing Hindu communal political interests.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hindu Mahasabha → Hindu Communal Political Organisation

63. Formation

  • The All-India Hindu Mahasabha developed into an organised all-India body in the second decade of the twentieth century.

64. Madan Mohan Malaviya

  • Madan Mohan Malaviya was among the important figures associated with early Hindu Mahasabha politics.

65. V.D. Savarkar

  • V.D. Savarkar later became one of the organisation's most influential ideological leaders.

66. Hindutva

  • Savarkar's work Hindutva was published in the early 1920s and articulated a political conception of Hindu identity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hindutva → V.D. Savarkar

67. Nehru Report

  • The Nehru Report was prepared in 1928 under Motilal Nehru.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nehru Report → Motilal Nehru → 1928

68. Background

  • It was prepared in response to the challenge to Indians to produce an agreed constitutional framework.

69. Dominion Status

  • The report proposed Dominion Status for India.

70. Joint Electorates

  • The Nehru Report generally favoured joint electorates rather than continuation of communal separate electorates.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nehru Report → Joint Electorates

71. Muslim Objections

  • Several Muslim political leaders believed the Nehru Report did not provide adequate safeguards.

72. Jinnah's Proposed Amendments

  • Jinnah proposed amendments designed to strengthen Muslim constitutional safeguards.

73. Failure of Agreement

  • Congress and major Muslim political representatives failed to reach a common constitutional settlement.

74. Jinnah's Fourteen Points

  • Jinnah formulated his Fourteen Points in 1929.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jinnah's Fourteen Points → 1929

75. Purpose

  • The Fourteen Points became a major statement of Muslim constitutional safeguards.

76. Federal Constitution

  • Jinnah demanded a federal structure with strong provincial autonomy.

77. Provincial Autonomy

  • Residual powers were to remain with provinces under his proposals.

78. Muslim Representation

  • Adequate Muslim representation in legislatures and government was a central demand.

79. Separate Electorates

  • Jinnah's Fourteen Points retained the demand for separate electorates unless communities agreed otherwise.

80. One-Third Representation

  • One-third Muslim representation in the Central Legislature was among the constitutional safeguards demanded.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fourteen Points → One-Third Muslim Representation at Centre

81. Sindh

  • Separation of Sindh from the Bombay Presidency was also supported.

82. NWFP and Baluchistan

  • Constitutional reforms for the North-West Frontier Province and Baluchistan were demanded.

83. Nehru Report vs Fourteen Points

Nehru Report:

  • Joint electorates.
  • Dominion Status.

Jinnah's Fourteen Points:

  • Strong Muslim safeguards.
  • Separate electorates retained.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

1928 → Nehru Report, 1929 → Jinnah's Fourteen Points

84. Muhammad Iqbal

  • Poet-philosopher Muhammad Iqbal became an important ideological figure in Muslim political thought.

85. Allahabad Address

  • Iqbal delivered his famous presidential address to the Muslim League at Allahabad in 1930.
📌 Must-Memorise

Allahabad Address → Muhammad Iqbal → 1930

86. Iqbal's Proposal

  • He discussed the consolidation of Muslim-majority provinces in north-western India into a political unit.

87. Important Caution

  • Iqbal's 1930 address should not simply be treated as identical to the later 1940 Pakistan Resolution.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Iqbal 1930 ≠ Lahore Resolution 1940

88. Round Table Conferences

  • Communal representation became a major issue during the Round Table Conferences held in London between 1930 and 1932.

89. Minority Question

  • Negotiations repeatedly failed to produce a generally accepted settlement on minority representation.

90. Communal Award

  • British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award in 1932.
📌 Must-Memorise

Communal Award → Ramsay MacDonald → 1932

91. Expanded Communal Representation

  • The Award continued and expanded separate communal representation for several groups.

92. Depressed Classes

  • It also proposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

93. Gandhi's Opposition

  • Gandhi opposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

94. Poona Pact

  • Gandhi's fast and negotiations with B.R. Ambedkar led to the Poona Pact in 1932.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poona Pact → Reserved Seats in Joint Electorates

95. Communal Award Significance

  • The Communal Award further entrenched community-based representation within colonial constitutional politics.

96. Choudhry Rahmat Ali

  • Choudhry Rahmat Ali became important for popularising the name "Pakistan."
📌 Must-Memorise

Pakistan Name → Choudhry Rahmat Ali

97. Now or Never

  • Rahmat Ali published the pamphlet Now or Never in 1933.
📌 Must-Memorise

Now or Never → 1933 → Rahmat Ali

98. "Pakistan"

  • The pamphlet used the name Pakistan for a proposed Muslim homeland in north-western India.

99. Word Pakistan

  • The name was constructed from geographical and political references to Muslim-majority regions.

100. Important Distinction

  • Rahmat Ali coined and promoted the name.
  • The Muslim League did not formally demand Pakistan in 1933.

101. Government of India Act 1935

  • The Government of India Act 1935 introduced major provincial constitutional changes.

102. Provincial Autonomy

  • Provincial autonomy became one of the Act's major features.

103. Separate Electorates Continued

  • Communal electorates remained part of the constitutional structure.

104. Sindh

  • Sindh was separated from the Bombay Presidency under the constitutional changes associated with the 1935 Act.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sindh Separated from Bombay Presidency → 1936 under 1935 Act Framework

105. 1937 Provincial Elections

  • Provincial elections were held in 1937 under the Government of India Act 1935.
📌 Must-Memorise

Provincial Elections → 1937

106. Congress Performance

  • Congress performed strongly and formed ministries in several provinces.

107. Muslim League Performance

  • The Muslim League did not yet dominate Muslim electoral politics across all Muslim-majority provinces.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

1937 → League Had Not Yet Become Sole Muslim Political Voice

108. Punjab

  • In Punjab, regional Muslim political organisations remained powerful.

109. Bengal

  • Bengal also had strong regional political forces outside the League.

110. League's Political Challenge

  • Jinnah therefore worked after 1937 to transform the League into a broader mass Muslim political organisation.

111. Congress Ministries

  • Congress ministries governed several provinces from 1937 to 1939.

112. League Criticism

  • The Muslim League accused Congress ministries of policies harmful to Muslim interests.

113. Pirpur Report

  • The League-sponsored Pirpur Report of 1938 criticised the record of Congress provincial ministries.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pirpur Report → Muslim League Criticism of Congress Ministries

114. Congress Rejection

  • Congress rejected many of these allegations.

115. Political Consequence

  • The controversy increased Congress-League distrust.

116. World War II

  • World War II began in September 1939.

117. India at War

  • Viceroy Lord Linlithgow declared India at war without consulting Indian elected representatives.

118. Congress Ministries Resign

  • Congress ministries resigned in 1939.
📌 Must-Memorise

Congress Ministries Resigned → 1939

119. Day of Deliverance

  • Jinnah called upon Muslims to observe 22 December 1939 as a "Day of Deliverance" from Congress rule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Day of Deliverance → 22 December 1939 → Jinnah

120. Political Polarisation

  • The resignation of Congress ministries further widened the political distance between Congress and the League.

121. Two-Nation Idea

  • By the late 1930s and early 1940s, the Muslim League increasingly argued that Hindus and Muslims constituted distinct political nations.

122. Two-Nation Theory

  • The Two-Nation Theory became a central ideological justification for the demand for separate Muslim statehood.
📌 Must-Memorise

Two-Nation Theory → Central to Later Muslim League Pakistan Demand

123. Important Caution

  • Ideas of separate Hindu and Muslim nationhood developed through multiple intellectual and political streams.
  • They should not be reduced to a single speech or one individual.

124. Lahore Session of Muslim League

  • The Muslim League held its historic Lahore session in March 1940.
📌 Must-Memorise

Muslim League Lahore Session → 1940

125. Lahore Resolution

  • The Lahore Resolution was adopted on 23 March 1940.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lahore Resolution → 23 March 1940

126. A.K. Fazlul Huq

  • A.K. Fazlul Huq, Premier of Bengal, moved the Lahore Resolution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lahore Resolution Moved By → A.K. Fazlul Huq

127. Muhammad Ali Jinnah

  • Jinnah provided the principal political leadership of the Muslim League at the session.

128. Muslim-Majority Zones

  • The resolution referred to Muslim-majority areas in the north-western and eastern zones of India.

129. "Independent States"

  • It called for these areas to be grouped into "independent states" in which constituent units would be autonomous and sovereign.

130. Word Pakistan

  • The word "Pakistan" did not appear in the text of the Lahore Resolution.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite Trap

Lahore Resolution → Pakistan Demand Context, But Word "Pakistan" → Not in Resolution

131. Pakistan Resolution

  • The Lahore Resolution later became popularly known as the Pakistan Resolution.

132. Importance

  • It marked the decisive shift of the Muslim League from constitutional safeguards within a united India toward territorial political separation.

133. August Offer

  • The British government announced the August Offer in 1940.

134. Minority Consent

  • British constitutional proposals increasingly emphasised that no future constitution would be imposed on large unwilling minorities.

135. Political Effect

  • This strengthened the League's bargaining position.

136. Cripps Mission

  • Sir Stafford Cripps came to India in 1942.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cripps Mission → 1942

137. Post-War Dominion

  • The Cripps proposals offered Dominion Status after the war.

138. Provincial Option

  • Provinces were given the possibility of not joining the proposed Indian Union.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cripps Proposals → Provincial Opt-Out Principle

139. Congress Rejection

  • Congress rejected the proposals as inadequate.

140. Muslim League Rejection

  • The Muslim League also rejected the proposals because they did not concede its full Pakistan demand.

141. Quit India

  • Congress launched the Quit India Movement in August 1942.

142. League Position

  • The Muslim League did not join the Quit India Movement.

143. Wartime Political Expansion

  • During Congress repression and leadership imprisonment, the Muslim League expanded its organisational influence.

144. Rajagopalachari Formula

  • C. Rajagopalachari proposed a formula in 1944 to resolve the Congress-League deadlock.
📌 Must-Memorise

C.R. Formula → Rajagopalachari → 1944

145. Main Idea

  • It proposed that the League support Indian independence and that the future of Muslim-majority areas be decided through a plebiscite after British withdrawal.

146. Demarcation

  • Contiguous Muslim-majority districts in the north-west and east were to be identified.

147. Plebiscite

  • The people in those areas would vote on separation.

148. Common Matters

  • If partition occurred, agreements would be needed on matters such as:
    • Defence.
    • Commerce.
    • Communication.

149. Gandhi–Jinnah Talks

  • Gandhi and Jinnah held extensive talks in 1944.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi–Jinnah Talks → 1944

150. Failure

  • The talks failed to produce an agreement.

151. Main Disagreement

  • Congress and League disagreed fundamentally over:
    • Whether India already consisted of two nations.
    • Timing of partition.
    • Territorial basis.
    • Authority to decide separation.

152. Wavell Plan

  • Viceroy Lord Wavell proposed a new political arrangement in 1945.
📌 Must-Memorise

Wavell Plan → 1945

153. Simla Conference

  • Indian leaders met at Simla in 1945 to discuss the Wavell Plan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Simla Conference → 1945

154. Executive Council

  • The plan sought to reconstitute the Viceroy's Executive Council with greater Indian participation.

155. League's Claim

  • Jinnah insisted that the Muslim League should have the exclusive right to nominate Muslim members.

156. Congress Position

  • Congress rejected the claim that the League alone represented all Indian Muslims.

157. Failure of Simla Conference

  • The disagreement contributed to the failure of the Simla Conference.

158. 1945 Central Elections

  • Elections to the Central Legislative Assembly were held in 1945.

159. League's Muslim Mandate

  • The Muslim League won all the Muslim seats in the Central Legislative Assembly.
📌 Must-Memorise

1945 Central Elections → League Won All Muslim Seats

160. 1946 Provincial Elections

  • Provincial elections followed in 1946.

161. League Performance

  • The League won the overwhelming majority of seats reserved for Muslims.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

1945–46 Elections → League Emerged as Dominant Muslim Electoral Organisation

162. Congress Performance

  • Congress won a dominant share of general constituencies.

163. Political Polarisation

  • The election results produced two competing claims:
    • Congress → Representative of Indian nationalism.
    • League → Representative of Muslim political opinion.

164. Cabinet Mission

  • A British Cabinet Mission arrived in India in March 1946.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cabinet Mission → 1946

165. Three Members

The Cabinet Mission consisted of:

  • Lord Pethick-Lawrence.
  • Sir Stafford Cripps.
  • A.V. Alexander.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cabinet Mission Trio → Pethick-Lawrence + Cripps + A.V. Alexander

166. Main Objective

  • The Mission attempted to devise a constitutional arrangement that would:
    • Preserve Indian unity.
    • Accommodate Muslim League concerns.
    • Transfer power.

167. Pakistan Rejected

  • The Cabinet Mission rejected the demand for a fully sovereign Pakistan as impractical in the proposed form.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cabinet Mission → Rejected Full Pakistan Demand

168. Limited Union

  • It proposed an Indian Union controlling:
    • Defence.
    • Foreign affairs.
    • Communications.

169. Provincial Powers

  • Most other powers would remain with provinces.

170. Provincial Groups

  • Provinces were to be organised into three sections or groups.

171. Group A

  • Group A consisted mainly of Hindu-majority provinces.

172. Group B

  • Group B consisted of Muslim-majority north-western provinces.

173. Group C

  • Group C consisted of Bengal and Assam.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cabinet Mission Groups → A + B + C

174. Constituent Assembly

  • The Mission proposed the creation of a Constituent Assembly.

175. Interim Government

  • It also proposed an interim government.

176. Congress Response

  • Congress accepted participation in the Constituent Assembly but interpreted provincial grouping differently from the League.

177. League Response

  • The Muslim League initially accepted the Cabinet Mission Plan.

178. League Withdrawal

  • The League later withdrew its acceptance after disagreements over interpretation.

179. Direct Action

  • The Muslim League decided to resort to Direct Action to press its Pakistan demand.
📌 Must-Memorise

Direct Action → Muslim League → 1946

180. Direct Action Day

  • Direct Action Day was observed on 16 August 1946.
📌 Must-Memorise

Direct Action Day → 16 August 1946

181. Calcutta

  • Calcutta became the centre of massive communal violence following Direct Action Day.

182. Great Calcutta Killings

  • The violence is commonly known as the Great Calcutta Killings.
📌 Must-Memorise

Great Calcutta Killings → August 1946

183. Communal Violence

  • Hindu and Muslim communities suffered heavy casualties.

184. Cycle of Violence

  • Communal violence subsequently spread to other regions.

185. Noakhali

  • Severe communal violence occurred in Noakhali in Bengal in October 1946.
📌 Must-Memorise

Noakhali → 1946 Communal Violence

186. Gandhi in Noakhali

  • Gandhi travelled through affected villages in Noakhali attempting to restore peace and communal confidence.

187. Bihar

  • Retaliatory communal violence occurred in Bihar in late 1946.

188. Punjab

  • Punjab became the most dangerous centre of communal conflict during the final months before Partition.

189. Interim Government

  • An Interim Government headed by Jawaharlal Nehru took office on 2 September 1946.
📌 Must-Memorise

Interim Government → 2 September 1946 → Nehru

190. League Initially Outside

  • The Muslim League initially remained outside the Interim Government.

191. League Joins

  • League representatives joined the Interim Government in October 1946.

192. Liaquat Ali Khan

  • Liaquat Ali Khan became an important League member of the Interim Government and held the Finance portfolio.
📌 Must-Memorise

Liaquat Ali Khan → Finance Member in Interim Government

193. Constituent Assembly

  • The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946.
📌 Must-Memorise

Constituent Assembly First Meeting → 9 December 1946

194. League Boycott

  • The Muslim League boycotted the initial meetings of the Constituent Assembly.

195. Constitutional Deadlock

  • By early 1947, attempts to preserve a united constitutional structure were rapidly collapsing.

196. Attlee Announcement

  • British Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced on 20 February 1947 that power would be transferred to Indian hands.
📌 Must-Memorise

Attlee Announcement → 20 February 1947

197. Deadline

  • Britain initially intended to transfer power no later than June 1948.

198. Lord Mountbatten

  • Lord Louis Mountbatten became the last Viceroy of British India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Last Viceroy → Lord Mountbatten

199. Mountbatten Arrives

  • Mountbatten arrived in India in March 1947.

200. Political Situation

He confronted:

  • Congress-League deadlock.
  • Communal violence.
  • Breakdown of administration in Punjab.
  • Increasing pressure for rapid transfer of power.

201. Punjab Crisis

  • Punjab contained large Muslim, Sikh and Hindu populations.
  • Any partition therefore carried enormous human and territorial consequences.

202. Bengal Crisis

  • Bengal also contained large Hindu and Muslim populations and faced the prospect of division.

203. Congress and Partition

  • Congress leaders who had long opposed partition gradually accepted it as the practical alternative to prolonged civil conflict and political deadlock.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Congress Acceptance of Partition → Reluctant Political Settlement

204. Gandhi's Position

  • Gandhi remained deeply opposed to communal division and continued to emphasise Hindu-Muslim unity.

205. Jinnah's Position

  • Jinnah and the Muslim League insisted on the establishment of Pakistan.

206. 3 June Plan

  • The British government announced the Mountbatten Plan on 3 June 1947.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mountbatten Plan / 3 June Plan → 3 June 1947

207. Partition Accepted

  • The Plan accepted partition as the basis for the transfer of power.

208. Punjab Partition

  • The Punjab Legislative Assembly was to decide whether the province should be partitioned.

209. Bengal Partition

  • Bengal's legislative representatives were similarly required to decide the province's future.

210. Boundary Commissions

  • Boundary Commissions were to demarcate the new borders in Punjab and Bengal.

211. Sindh

  • The Sindh Legislative Assembly was empowered to determine the province's constitutional choice.

212. North-West Frontier Province

  • A referendum was provided for the North-West Frontier Province.
📌 Must-Memorise

NWFP → Referendum → 1947

213. Ghaffar Khan

  • Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and his allies opposed the terms of the NWFP referendum and boycotted it.

214. Sylhet Referendum

  • A referendum was held in Sylhet to determine whether it would remain with Assam or join East Bengal.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sylhet → Referendum → 1947

215. Result of Sylhet Referendum

  • Most of Sylhet joined East Bengal, while some areas remained with Assam.

216. Congress Acceptance

  • Congress formally accepted the 3 June Plan.

217. League Acceptance

  • The Muslim League also accepted the Plan.

218. Sikh Leadership

  • Sikh political leaders accepted partition despite major concerns over Punjab's division.

219. Indian Independence Bill

  • Legislation implementing the plan was introduced in the British Parliament.

220. Indian Independence Act

  • The Indian Independence Act received Royal Assent on 18 July 1947.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Independence Act → 18 July 1947

221. Two Dominions

  • The Act created two independent Dominions:
    • India.
    • Pakistan.

222. Appointed Day

  • Under the Act, 15 August 1947 was the appointed date for the creation of the two Dominions.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Pakistan Celebrates Independence on 14 August, Indian Independence Act's Appointed Day → 15 August 1947

223. British Paramountcy

  • British paramountcy over princely states lapsed with independence.

224. End of British Rule

  • The Act ended British legislative authority over the two new Dominions.

225. Pakistan

  • Pakistan comprised:
    • Western territories.
    • Eastern Bengal territory.
  • These two wings were geographically separated by Indian territory.

226. East Pakistan

  • Eastern Bengal later became East Pakistan.

227. Bangladesh

  • East Pakistan became the independent state of Bangladesh in 1971.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

East Bengal → East Pakistan → Bangladesh

228. Boundary Commission

  • Separate boundary commissions were established for:
    • Punjab.
    • Bengal.

229. Sir Cyril Radcliffe

  • Sir Cyril Radcliffe chaired both boundary commissions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Radcliffe → Boundary of Punjab and Bengal

230. Radcliffe Line

  • The boundaries drawn during Partition became known as the Radcliffe Line.
📌 Must-Memorise

Radcliffe Line → India–Pakistan Partition Boundary

231. Basis of Boundary

  • Religious majorities were an important criterion, along with other considerations.

232. Difficulty

  • Districts contained:
    • Mixed populations.
    • Economic links.
    • Irrigation systems.
    • Railway connections.
  • This made boundary-making extremely difficult.

233. Radcliffe Award

  • The final boundary award was made public on 17 August 1947.
📌 Must-Memorise

Radcliffe Award Published → 17 August 1947

234. After Independence

  • The boundary became public only after India and Pakistan had formally achieved independence.

235. Punjab Division

  • Punjab was divided between:
    • India.
    • Pakistan.

236. Bengal Division

  • Bengal was divided between:
    • West Bengal in India.
    • East Bengal in Pakistan.

237. Lahore

  • Lahore became part of Pakistan.

238. Amritsar

  • Amritsar remained in India.

239. Calcutta

  • Calcutta remained in India.

240. Dacca

  • Dacca became part of East Bengal in Pakistan.

241. Mass Migration

  • Partition triggered one of the largest forced migrations of the twentieth century.

242. Population Movement

  • Millions of Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs crossed the newly created borders.

243. Punjab Migration

  • Migration was particularly rapid and violent across Punjab.

244. Bengal Migration

  • Bengal also experienced major population movement, although its pattern differed from Punjab.

245. Communal Massacres

  • Partition was accompanied by widespread communal massacres.

246. Refugees

  • Newly independent India and Pakistan faced enormous refugee rehabilitation challenges.

247. Women During Partition

  • Women were especially vulnerable to:
    • Abduction.
    • Sexual violence.
    • Forced conversion.
    • Forced marriage.
    • Displacement.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Partition → Political Division + Massive Human Tragedy

248. Property Loss

  • Families lost:
    • Homes.
    • Land.
    • Businesses.
    • Personal property.

249. Administrative Disruption

  • Partition required division of:
    • Civil services.
    • Military assets.
    • Financial resources.
    • Government records.
    • Transport systems.

250. Gandhi in Calcutta

  • Gandhi concentrated on communal peace rather than participating in formal independence celebrations in Delhi.

251. Calcutta Peace Efforts

  • His peace efforts in Calcutta helped reduce communal violence temporarily.

252. Gandhi in Noakhali

  • Gandhi had earlier walked through Noakhali villages attempting reconciliation after the 1946 violence.

253. Gandhi in Delhi

  • After Partition, Gandhi worked to reduce communal violence in Delhi and protect minorities.

254. Gandhi's Fast

  • Gandhi also used fasting to pressure communities and political authorities toward restoration of communal peace.

255. Jinnah as Pakistan's Leader

  • Muhammad Ali Jinnah became the first Governor-General of Pakistan.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Governor-General of Pakistan → Muhammad Ali Jinnah

256. Liaquat Ali Khan

  • Liaquat Ali Khan became Pakistan's first Prime Minister.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Prime Minister of Pakistan → Liaquat Ali Khan

257. India

  • Jawaharlal Nehru became independent India's first Prime Minister.

258. Mountbatten

  • Mountbatten became the first Governor-General of independent India.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Governor-General of Independent India → Lord Mountbatten

259. Rajagopalachari

  • C. Rajagopalachari later became the first and only Indian Governor-General of India.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

First Governor-General of Independent India → Mountbatten, First Indian Governor-General → Rajaji

260. Communalism's Political Consequence

  • By 1947, communal political polarisation had moved from demands for safeguards to territorial partition.

261. Constitutional Evolution

The broad constitutional sequence was:

Separate representation → Separate electorates → Communal safeguards → Competing national claims → Territorial partition.

262. Simla Deputation to Pakistan

The political sequence can be remembered as:

1906 Simla Deputation → 1906 Muslim League → 1909 Separate Electorates → 1916 Lucknow Pact → 1929 Fourteen Points → 1930 Iqbal Address → 1933 Pakistan Name → 1940 Lahore Resolution → 1947 Partition.

263. Muslim League's Evolution

The League moved broadly from:

Protection of Muslim political interests → Constitutional safeguards → Claim to represent Indian Muslims → Demand for separate statehood.

264. Congress Position

  • Congress officially presented itself as a secular national organisation representing Indians across religious communities.
  • It rejected the claim that religious communities necessarily constituted separate nations.

265. Congress and Separate Electorates

  • Congress accepted separate electorates temporarily in the Lucknow Pact but later increasingly favoured joint political nationalism.

266. Jinnah's Evolution

Jinnah's political career moved through:

  • Constitutional nationalism.
  • Congress-League cooperation.
  • Muslim constitutional safeguards.
  • Muslim League leadership.
  • Pakistan demand.

267. Iqbal vs Rahmat Ali vs Jinnah

  • Muhammad Iqbal → Allahabad Address, 1930.
  • Choudhry Rahmat Ali → Pakistan name, 1933.
  • Muhammad Ali Jinnah → Political leadership of Pakistan demand.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Do Not Interchange These Three

268. Lahore Resolution vs Mountbatten Plan

Lahore Resolution:

  • Muslim League political demand.
  • 1940.

Mountbatten Plan:

  • British transfer-of-power plan accepting partition.
  • 1947.

269. Cabinet Mission vs Mountbatten Plan

Cabinet Mission:

  • Tried to preserve a united India.
  • 1946.

Mountbatten Plan:

  • Accepted partition.
  • 1947.
📌 Must-Memorise

1946 → Unity Attempt, 1947 → Partition Plan

270. Lucknow Pact vs Lahore Resolution

Lucknow Pact:

  • Congress-League cooperation.
  • 1916.

Lahore Resolution:

  • League movement toward territorial separation.
  • 1940.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Lucknow → Cooperation, Lahore → Separation

271. Separate Electorates vs Partition

  • Separate electorates did not automatically mean partition.
  • However, they strengthened community-based political representation that later became one factor in deeper political separation.

272. Colonial Responsibility

  • British constitutional policies institutionalised communal electorates and frequently managed Indian politics through community categories.

273. Indian Political Responsibility

  • Indian political organisations and leaders also made choices that deepened communal polarisation.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Partition → Multiple Causes, Not a Single Cause

274. Economic and Social Factors

  • Competition for:
    • Government employment.
    • Education.
    • Representation.
    • Local political influence also interacted with religious identity.

275. Provincial Differences

  • Communal politics differed significantly between:
    • Punjab.
    • Bengal.
    • United Provinces.
    • Bombay.
    • Madras.
  • It should not be treated as identical everywhere.

276. Punjab

  • Punjab's politics involved Muslims, Sikhs and Hindus as well as powerful regional interests.

277. Bengal

  • Bengal's politics combined:
    • Religious identity.
    • Agrarian interests.
    • Regional politics.
    • Language and culture.

278. Madras Presidency

  • Communal politics in the Madras Presidency developed differently from the intense Hindu-Muslim territorial conflict seen in Punjab and Bengal.

279. Minority Safeguards

  • One of the central unresolved constitutional questions throughout the late colonial period was how minority rights should be protected in a democratic India.

280. Failure of Power-Sharing

  • Congress and the League ultimately failed to agree on a durable system of all-India power-sharing.

281. Timing of British Withdrawal

  • Britain's decision to accelerate transfer of power reduced the time available for:
    • Administrative preparation.
    • Boundary settlement.
    • Population protection.

282. Boundary Uncertainty

  • Uncertainty over the final Punjab and Bengal boundaries increased fear and migration.

283. Human Cost

  • The human cost of Partition cannot be understood only through constitutional plans and political agreements.
  • It involved large-scale:
    • Death.
    • Migration.
    • Trauma.
    • Family separation.

284. Long-Term Consequence

  • Partition created India and Pakistan as separate states and permanently transformed South Asian politics.

285. Kashmir

  • The princely-state question, especially Jammu and Kashmir, became a major India-Pakistan dispute after Partition.
  • It arose from the separate issue of princely-state accession rather than the Radcliffe partition of British Indian provinces.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Punjab/Bengal → Radcliffe Boundary, Princely States → Accession Process

286. Hyderabad and Junagadh

  • Hyderabad and Junagadh were also princely-state accession questions, not territories divided directly by the Radcliffe Award.

287. Main Political Organisations

  • All-India Muslim League.
  • Hindu Mahasabha.

Who became Pakistan's first Governor-General? → Muhammad Ali Jinnah.

Who became Pakistan's first Prime Minister? → Liaquat Ali Khan.

Who became India's first Prime Minister? → Jawaharlal Nehru.

Who became independent India's first Governor-General? → Lord Mountbatten.

Who later became the first Indian Governor-General? → C. Rajagopalachari.

What is the easiest Iqbal–Rahmat Ali–Jinnah distinction? → Iqbal–Allahabad Address; Rahmat Ali–Pakistan name; Jinnah–political leadership of Pakistan demand.

What is the easiest Lucknow–Lahore distinction? → Lucknow 1916 represented Congress-League cooperation; Lahore 1940 represented the League's move toward territorial separation.

What is the easiest Cabinet Mission–Mountbatten distinction? → Cabinet Mission 1946 tried to preserve Indian unity; Mountbatten Plan 1947 accepted Partition.

What is the central TNPSC takeaway? → Communal politics evolved gradually from demands for separate representation into competing claims of nationhood. The Simla Deputation and Morley–Minto separate electorates institutionalised community-based politics; the Lucknow Pact temporarily united Congress and League; later constitutional disagreements, the Fourteen Points, the Lahore Resolution and League electoral consolidation intensified separation; failure of the Cabinet Mission, Direct Action and communal violence destroyed prospects for agreed power-sharing; and the Mountbatten Plan and Indian Independence Act ultimately created India and Pakistan in 1947 at enormous human cost.
